title: Binary Search — Complete OA Mastery Guide
subtitle: All Variations + DS Combinations | FAANG & Hard OA Prep
author: Mayank | IIIT Kottayam
overview:
Binary Search is not just "find element in sorted array". It is a **divide-and-conquer decision framework** — any time you can define a *monotone predicate* on a search space, binary search applies. This document covers:

1. **Pure Binary Search Variations** — classic, answer space, rotated arrays, 2D, bounds
2. **BS + Other DS Combos** — Prefix Sum, Greedy, Two Pointers, BIT/Segment Tree, Heap, Graph/BFS, Trie, DSU, DP
coreConcept:
Binary search works by maintaining an invariant: the answer lies in [lo, hi]. At each step, we evaluate the midpoint and **eliminate half the search space** by deciding which half cannot contain the answer.

The key insight: you don't need a sorted array — you need a **monotone predicate** f(x) such that f(x) is false while x < answer and true once x >= answer. Binary search finds the **first x where f(x) is true**.

foundationTemplates.label: Universal Binary Search Template

foundationTricks: **The Golden Rule**: If the search space is monotone (all `false` then all `true`, or vice versa), binary search works.
**Template choice**: Use `lo < hi` with `mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2` to avoid overflow and infinite loops.
**On Answer**: When problem says "minimize the maximum" or "maximize the minimum" — binary search on the answer, not the array.
**Off-by-one**: The most common bug. Always trace through a 2-element array before submitting.
**Real-valued BS**: Use a fixed loop count (~100 iterations) instead of `lo < hi` when the answer is a floating point.

triggerWords: "sorted array", "rotated sorted array" → Classic / Rotated BS
"minimum maximum", "maximize the minimum", "at least k" → BS on Answer
"kth smallest/largest" → BS on Answer or BS + Heap/BIT
"count inversions" → BS + BIT (Merge Sort or BIT approach)
structureSignals: Answer has a clear lower and upper bound
Checking if a value is "feasible" can be done in O(n) or O(n log n)
Monotone relationship: if x works, x+1 works (or vice versa)

variationsSummary.complexity: O(k log n) or O(n log(range))

commonMistakes: **Integer overflow**: Always use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, never `(lo + hi) / 2`.
**Infinite loop**: Using `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` with `lo = mid` (not `mid + 1`) can loop forever. Use upper mid `lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2` when `lo = mid`.
**Off-by-one in bounds**: When returning `lo` vs `lo - 1`, trace through 1 and 2 element examples.
**Wrong feasibility direction**: Ensure you know whether larger value = more feasible or less feasible.
**Long overflow in sum**: Use `long` for prefix sums and multiplicative bounds.
**Duplicates in rotated array**: LC 81 worst case becomes O(n) with duplicates.
**Coordinate compression in BIT**: Map values to [1, n] before BIT operations.
**LIS strictly increasing vs non-decreasing**: Lower bound vs upper bound in patience sorting.
**Trie bit order**: Always process from MSB (bit 31 or 30) to LSB (bit 0).
interviewTips: **State the predicate first**: Before coding, explicitly say "I'll binary search on x; my predicate is f(x) = can we achieve x?"
**Verify monotonicity**: Confirm out loud that if x is feasible, x+1 is also feasible (or vice versa).
**Set bounds carefully**: Lower bound = minimum possible answer, upper bound = maximum possible answer. Think about these before writing the loop.
**Template discipline**: Use the same template every time. Fewer bugs under pressure.
**Feasibility before optimization**: Get the greedy/BFS check working first, then wrap in BS.
**Trace small cases**: Always trace through array of size 1 and 2 to catch off-by-one.
**For OAs**: When you see "minimum maximum" or "maximum minimum" or allocation/partition problems — immediately think BS on Answer.
priorityLegend: **[MUST]** — Do these first. Core patterns that appear in almost every company OA. If you only have limited time, these 12 problems are your entire preparation.
**[GOOD]** — Do these after MUST. Solidify the pattern, cover common variants. High ROI.
**[SKIP]** — Only if you have extra time or targeting DE Shaw / competitive programming. Low probability in standard product company OAs.
targetAdvice: **Razorpay / Shipsy**: MUST list is fully sufficient. They heavily favour BS on Answer + Greedy (allocation, capacity, scheduling problems). Rarely go beyond that.
**DE Shaw**: Do MUST + GOOD. They can ask BS + BIT (inversions, count smaller) and harder combos.
**NVIDIA**: MUST list + LC 300 (LIS). Their OA is fairly standard SDE, not competitive-programming hard.
**General rule**: 12 problems done deeply > 35 problems done surface-level.
closingNote: Do the 12 MUSTs properly — understand the predicate, set bounds correctly, write the feasibility function without bugs. That covers ~90% of what Razorpay, Shipsy, and NVIDIA will throw at you. Add the GOOD list for DE Shaw. The SKIP list exists for completeness — don't feel pressured to do them before placements.

variations.name: Classic Binary Search
variations.coreIdea: Find a target value in a sorted array. The invariant: target is always in [lo, hi].

items: Array must be sorted (or have a clear monotone property)
At each step, `mid` is compared to target to eliminate half
Always use `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` to prevent integer overflow
Return -1 if `lo > hi` after loop
**Never use `(lo+hi)/2`**: Overflows when both are large integers. Use `lo + (hi-lo)/2`.
**Loop condition**: `lo <= hi` for exact match; `lo < hi` for bound-finding.
**When to return mid**: Only when `arr[mid] == target` for classic search.

solved.title: Binary Search
solved.statement: Given a sorted array `nums` and target, return index of target or -1.

items: Array is sorted ⇒ we can eliminate half at each step
If `nums[mid] < target`, answer must be to the right
If `nums[mid] > target`, answer must be to the left

boxes.body: Maintain invariant: target is in [lo, hi]. Evaluate midpoint each time to shrink the window. When `lo > hi`, target doesn't exist.

optimal.approach: Classic two-pointer binary search.

solved.title: Sqrt(x)
solved.statement: Given integer x, return floor of sqrt(x) without using sqrt().

items: Answer lies in [0, x] (or [0, x/2+1] for x > 1)
We want the largest m such that m^2 <= x
This is a lower/upper bound problem on answer space

boxes.body: Binary search on [1, x]. For each `mid`, check if `mid*mid <= x`. We want the last `mid` where this is true — so when `mid*mid <= x`, record answer and go right; else go left.

optimal.approach: Binary search on the answer with a long guard against overflow.

variations.name: Lower Bound / Upper Bound
variations.coreIdea: **Lower Bound**: first index where `arr[i] >= target`. **Upper Bound**: first index where `arr[i] > target`. Count of target = `upperBound(target) - lowerBound(target)`.

items: Both use the template `lo < hi` with `hi = mid` when condition met
Lower bound: condition is `arr[mid] >= target`
Upper bound: condition is `arr[mid] > target`
After loop, `lo` is the answer
**Count occurrences**: `ub(x) - lb(x)` gives exact count in O(log n)
**Floor/Ceil**: `lb(x) - 1` gives floor, `lb(x)` gives ceil
**Java**: Use `Arrays.binarySearch()` then check sign for existence; manual for bounds.

problems.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array

solved.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
solved.statement: Given sorted array and target, find first and last index of target. Return [-1,-1] if not found.

items: First occurrence = lower bound of target
Last occurrence = upper bound of target - 1
Two separate binary searches needed

boxes.body: Run lower bound to find first position >= target. If that position has the target, it's the first occurrence. Run upper bound to find first position > target; subtract 1 for last occurrence.

optimal.approach: Two bound searches.

solved.title: Kth Missing Positive Number
solved.statement: Given sorted positive array `arr` and integer k, find the kth missing positive integer.

items: Missing count before `arr[i]` = `arr[i] - (i+1)`
This count is monotonically increasing ⇒ binary search applies
Find first index where missing count >= k

boxes.body: If no elements were missing, position i should hold value i+1. `arr[i] - (i+1)` gives missing count before `arr[i]`. Binary search for the first index where this count >= k. Answer is `lo + k` (lo is the number of elements before the kth missing).

optimal.approach: Binary search on the missing-count function.

variations.name: Binary Search on Answer Space
variations.coreIdea: Instead of searching an array, we search the **space of possible answers**. Define a predicate `feasible(x)` that checks if answer x is achievable. The predicate is monotone.

items: Identify: what is the minimum / maximum of what?
Set `lo` = smallest possible answer, `hi` = largest possible answer
Write `feasible(x)`: can we achieve answer <= x (or >= x)?
Binary search for the boundary where feasible flips from false to true
**"Minimize the maximum"**: `feasible(x)` = can we keep all values <= x?
**"Maximize the minimum"**: `feasible(x)` = can we keep all values >= x?
**Bounds**: lo = min possible (often 1 or `max(arr)`), hi = max possible (often `sum(arr)`)
**Greedy check**: `feasible()` is almost always a greedy scan O(n)

solved.title: Split Array Largest Sum
solved.statement: Split array into m non-empty subarrays to minimize the largest sum among them.

items: Answer lies in [max(nums), sum(nums)]
If maximum allowed sum is x, greedily pack elements until sum exceeds x, count groups
If groups needed <= m, then x is feasible
Feasibility is monotone: if x works, x+1 works ⇒ binary search on x

boxes.body: Binary search on the answer (the largest sum). For a given limit x, greedily scan the array and count how many partitions we need. If partitions <= m, x is feasible and we try smaller. Else try larger.

optimal.approach: Binary search on answer + greedy feasibility.

complexity.timeNote: O(n) feasibility check, O(log S) iterations

solved.title: Aggressive Cows
solved.statement: Place c cows in n stalls (given positions) such that the minimum distance between any two cows is maximized.

items: Answer is the minimum distance, which we want to maximize
Answer lies in [1, stalls[n-1] - stalls[0]]
For a given min distance d, greedily place cows as far right as possible
Sort stalls first — placement only makes sense on sorted positions

boxes.body: "Maximize the minimum" ⇒ binary search on the answer (the minimum distance). For each candidate distance d, check if we can place all c cows with gaps >= d by greedily placing from left to right.

optimal.approach: Binary search on the answer with upper-mid to avoid an infinite loop when maximizing.

variations.name: Binary Search on Rotated / Modified Array
variations.coreIdea: A sorted array is rotated at some pivot. One half is always sorted — use this property to decide which half to search.

items: One of the two halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is always sorted
Check which half is sorted by comparing `nums[lo]` and `nums[mid]`
If target is in the sorted half, go there; else go to the other half
For duplicates (LC 81), `lo++` when `nums[lo] == nums[mid]`

solved.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
solved.statement: Search for target in a rotated sorted array (no duplicates). Return index or -1.

items: If `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`, left half [lo, mid] is sorted
Otherwise, right half [mid, hi] is sorted
Check if target falls in the sorted half; if yes, search there; else search the other half

boxes.body: Even in a rotated array, at least one half around mid is always sorted. Identify which half is sorted, check if target belongs there, and binary search within.

optimal.approach: Identify the sorted half at each step.

solved.title: Single Element in a Sorted Array
solved.statement: Every element appears exactly twice except one. Find the single element. Must run in O(log n).

items: Array is sorted with all duplicates paired: `[1,1,2,2,3,3,4,4,5]`
Before the single element: pairs start at **even** indices (`nums[i] == nums[i+1]` for even i)
After the single element: pairs start at **odd** indices (`nums[i] == nums[i+1]` for odd i)
This parity flip is the monotone predicate — binary search on it
Always keep `lo` and `hi` on even indices to simplify logic

boxes.body: In a perfectly paired array with no single element, every pair starts at an even index. The single element breaks this pattern — everything to its right shifts by one, so pairs start at odd indices. Binary search for the first position where this parity flip occurs. Keep `mid` always even (round down to nearest even) to consistently check: does `nums[mid] == nums[mid+1]`? If yes, the single element is to the right (`lo = mid + 2`). If no, it's at `mid` or to the left (`hi = mid`).

bruteForce.approach: XOR all elements, or scan pairs.

optimal.approach: Binary search on index parity.

variations.name: 2D Matrix Binary Search
variations.coreIdea: Treat a fully sorted matrix as a flattened 1D array, or walk the staircase from the top-right corner when rows and columns are sorted independently.

items: **LC 74**: Each row sorted, first element of next row > last of current ⇒ treat as 1D array, map index via `mid/cols` and `mid%cols`
**LC 240**: Each row and column sorted but not globally ⇒ start from top-right, move left if too big, move down if too small

solved.title: Search a 2D Matrix
solved.statement: Matrix where each row is sorted and first of next > last of current. Search for target.

optimal.approach: Index the matrix as a flat sorted array.

variations.name: BS + Prefix Sum
variations.coreIdea: Prefix sum arrays are monotonically non-decreasing (for non-negative inputs). Binary search on prefix sums to answer range queries like "find shortest subarray with sum >= k" or "count subarrays in sum range".

items: Prefix sum array P where `P[i] = A[0] + ... + A[i-1]` is sorted if all elements are non-negative
Subarray sum [l, r] = `P[r+1] - P[l]`
Binary search on P to find boundaries efficiently
For negative numbers: use a hashmap for exact sum, not binary search
When all elements are **positive**: prefix sum is sorted ⇒ BS applicable
**"Shortest subarray with sum >= k"**: for each right end, BS left end in prefix sums
**Count in range**: f(x) = number of prefix sums <= x, then answer = f(hi) - f(lo-1)

problems.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K

solved.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
solved.statement: Find minimum length subarray with sum >= target. All positive integers.

items: All positive ⇒ prefix sum is strictly increasing ⇒ BS works
For each right end r, find smallest l such that `P[r+1] - P[l] >= target`
Equivalently: find largest l such that `P[l] <= P[r+1] - target` via upper bound
Sliding window also works in O(n) — know both

boxes.body: Prefix sums are sorted (all elements positive). For each position r, we need `P[l] <= P[r+1] - target`. Binary search for the rightmost such l. Subarray length = r - l + 1.

The source's snippet for this problem contained a half-corrected inner binary search with contradictory comments; it is reproduced verbatim below. In practice use the sliding-window O(n) solution, or the `upperBound` helper alone.

optimal.approach: Prefix sums + upper bound per right endpoint (sliding window is O(n) and preferred).

complexity.timeNote: BS approach; sliding window gives O(n)

variations.name: BS + Greedy (Feasibility Check)
variations.coreIdea: The most powerful OA combo. Binary search on answer, verify feasibility using a greedy O(n) scan.

items: Works when feasibility is monotone: if x is feasible, x+1 is too (or vice versa)
Feasibility check is almost always a greedy linear scan
This pattern handles: allocation, scheduling, capacity, partitioning problems

solved.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
solved.statement: Find minimum ship capacity to ship all packages in D days in order.

items: Minimum capacity = `max(weights)` (must carry heaviest single package)
Maximum capacity = `sum(weights)` (carry all in one day)
For capacity x: greedily fill each day until next package would exceed x
If days needed <= D, capacity x is feasible

boxes.body: "Minimum capacity" ⇒ binary search on capacity. Feasibility check: simulate loading packages greedily, count days. This is monotone: larger capacity ⇒ fewer or equal days.

optimal.approach: Binary search on capacity + greedy day count.

solved.title: Minimum Time to Complete Trips
solved.statement: Given n buses each completing a trip in `time[i]`, find minimum time for all buses together to make >= totalTrips.

items: In time t, bus i completes floor(t / time[i]) trips
Total trips at time t = sum of floor(t / time[i]) — monotonically increasing in t
Binary search on time t

optimal.approach: Binary search on elapsed time.

variations.name: BS + Two Pointers
variations.coreIdea: Binary search on answer, verify feasibility using a two-pointer count in O(n).

items: Classic use: "Kth smallest pair distance" — binary search on distance d, count pairs with distance <= d using two pointers
Also: number of pairs satisfying a condition counted with two pointers

problems.title: Kth Smallest Number in Multiplication Table
Kth Largest Element in an Array

solved.title: Find K-th Smallest Pair Distance
solved.statement: Given array, find the kth smallest absolute difference among all pairs.

items: Sort the array first. Pair distances range from 0 to `nums[n-1] - nums[0]`
Binary search on answer d: count pairs with distance <= d
Count via two pointers on sorted array: for each right pointer r, find leftmost l such that `nums[r] - nums[l] <= d`
Find first d where count >= k

boxes.body: Sort the array. Binary search on the distance value d. For each candidate d, count pairs with distance <= d using two pointers in O(n). The count is monotone in d, so binary search for the smallest d where count >= k.

bruteForce.approach: Generate all pairs, sort, return kth.

optimal.approach: Binary search on distance + two-pointer counting.

complexity.time: O(n log n + n log W)

variations.name: BS + BIT / Segment Tree
variations.coreIdea: Use BIT (Binary Indexed Tree) or Segment Tree for dynamic frequency/sum tracking. Binary search on the BIT to find Kth elements or count inversions.

items: **Count inversions**: For each element, count elements already inserted that are greater. BIT stores frequency; query prefix sum.
**Kth smallest in stream**: Insert into BIT, binary search for first position where prefix count >= k
**BS on BIT**: Walk down BIT in O(log n) to find Kth element without extra binary search
**Coordinate compression**: BIT indexed by value ⇒ compress to [1, n] first
**BIT walk**: To find Kth element, walk BIT from MSB to LSB in O(log n)
**Merge sort**: Also counts inversions in O(n log n) — know both approaches

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

solved.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
solved.statement: For each element in array, count elements to its right that are smaller.

items: Process from right to left, inserting into BIT indexed by value
For current element x: query BIT for prefix sum [1, x-1] = count of smaller elements already seen (i.e., to the right)
Coordinate compress values to [1, n]

boxes.body: Maintain a BIT of frequencies. Traverse right to left. Before inserting current element, query "how many elements in BIT are < x?" (prefix sum up to x-1). This gives count of smaller to the right.

optimal.approach: Coordinate compression + Fenwick tree.

complexity.timeNote: n updates and queries each O(log n)

variations.name: BS + Heap
variations.coreIdea: For Kth smallest problems in matrices or across multiple sorted lists, binary search on value and use a heap to verify/count, or use heap-based extraction.

items: **Kth smallest in sorted matrix (LC 378)**: two approaches — min-heap extraction k times, O(k log n); or BS on value counting elements <= mid via row-wise walk, O(n log(range))
BS approach is better when k is large

solved.title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
solved.statement: n x n matrix with sorted rows and columns. Find Kth smallest element.

items: Binary search on value in [matrix[0][0], matrix[n-1][n-1]]
For each candidate `mid`, count elements <= `mid`
Count efficiently: start at top-right, move down if `matrix[r][c] <= mid`, else move left
Count = (row index + 1) accumulated = O(n) total

boxes.body: Binary search on the answer value. For candidate value x, count how many matrix elements are <= x in O(n) using the sorted-matrix staircase traversal. Find smallest x where count >= k.

optimal.approach: Binary search on value + staircase counting.

solved.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
solved.statement: Find median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m,n))).

items: Binary search on partition point of the smaller array
For partition at index i in `nums1`, partition in `nums2` at j = (m+n+1)/2 - i
Valid partition: `nums1[i-1] <= nums2[j]` and `nums2[j-1] <= nums1[i]`
Adjust i based on which condition fails

boxes.body: A valid median partition splits merged array into two halves of equal size. Binary search on the partition index of the smaller array. For each candidate partition in `nums1`, derive the required partition in `nums2`. Check if partition is valid; adjust if not.

optimal.approach: Binary search on the partition of the smaller array.

variations.name: BS + Graph / BFS
variations.coreIdea: Binary search on edge weight (or path cost), verify with BFS/DFS whether a valid path exists under that constraint.

items: **Minimum bottleneck path**: BS on max edge weight, BFS/DFS to check connectivity
**Path with minimum effort**: BS on effort, BFS/Dijkstra to verify
**Swim in rising water**: BS on water level, BFS to check reachability
All follow: define answer space → write feasibility BFS → binary search

solved.title: Path With Minimum Effort
solved.statement: Grid where each cell has a height. Move up/down/left/right. Effort = max absolute difference between consecutive cells. Find minimum effort to reach bottom-right from top-left.

items: Effort lies in [0, max(heights)]
For effort limit e: can we reach (n-1, m-1) using only edges with diff <= e?
BFS/DFS check: only traverse edges where `|h1 - h2| <= e`
Answer is monotone: larger e ⇒ more edges available ⇒ easier to reach

boxes.body: Binary search on the effort e. For each candidate, run a BFS treating only edges with height difference <= e as valid. If we can reach the destination, e is feasible and we try smaller; else try larger.

optimal.approach: Binary search on effort + BFS reachability.

variations.name: BS + DP (LIS Family)
variations.coreIdea: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) and its variants can be solved in O(n log n) using a "tails" array and binary search (patience sorting).

items: Maintain `tails[]` where `tails[i]` = smallest tail element of all increasing subsequences of length i+1
`tails[]` is always sorted ⇒ binary search applicable
For each element x: find first tail >= x (lower bound), replace it with x
Length of LIS = length of `tails[]` at the end
**Strictly increasing**: use lower bound (first >= x, replace with x)
**Non-decreasing**: use upper bound (first > x, replace with x)
**LCS via LIS**: For two sequences, LCS can reduce to LIS with coordinate compression
**Russian Dolls / 2D LIS**: Sort by one dimension, find LIS on the other
**Count LIS**: Requires BIT; just length uses patience sorting

problems.title: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference
Minimum Number of Removals to Make Mountain Array

solved.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
solved.statement: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

items: DP approach: O(n^2), `dp[i] = max(dp[j]+1)` for j < i, `nums[j] < nums[i]`
Patience sorting: Maintain sorted tails array. For each x, find first tail >= x (lower bound), replace. If x larger than all, append.
`tails.length` = LIS length

boxes.body: We maintain a virtual game of patience solitaire. `tails[i]` is the minimum possible tail for an increasing subsequence of length i+1. Smaller tails give more room for future extensions. Binary search finds where the current element fits in (or extends) these subsequences.

bruteForce.approach: Classic DP over all previous indices.

optimal.approach: Patience sorting with explicit lower-bound search.

complexity.timeNote: n elements, each with O(log n) binary search

solved.title: Russian Doll Envelopes
solved.statement: Envelopes with width w and height h. An envelope fits inside another if both w and h are strictly smaller. Find max envelopes you can nest.

items: This is 2D LIS
Sort by width ascending, then by height **descending** (crucial!)
Run LIS on heights only
Descending height for same width prevents using same-width envelopes in LIS

boxes.body: If we sort by width only and run LIS on heights, same-width envelopes could appear in our subsequence (wrong). By sorting height descending for same width, when we run LIS on heights, we can pick at most one envelope per width — automatically handling the strict requirement.

optimal.approach: Sort width asc / height desc, then LIS on heights.

variations.name: BS + Trie (XOR Maximization)
variations.coreIdea: Insert numbers bit by bit into a binary trie. For XOR maximization, at each bit try to go the opposite direction. Binary search on the answer (XOR value) with trie verification.

items: Trie stores binary representations of numbers (bit 30 to bit 0)
For max XOR with query q: at each bit, try the opposite bit of q in trie
If opposite exists, take it (sets that bit in XOR to 1); else take same direction
BS variant: binary search on the answer XOR value, verify existence in trie

solved.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
solved.statement: Find maximum XOR of any two numbers in the array.

items: Greedy bit-by-bit: try to set each bit of result to 1 from MSB to LSB
At each bit level, check if two numbers in prefix set can achieve this bit as 1
Trie approach: insert all, then query each number for max XOR

optimal.approach: Binary trie with greedy opposite-bit descent.

variations.name: BS + DSU (Kruskal's / Connectivity)
variations.coreIdea: Sort edges by weight, use DSU to add edges incrementally. Binary search on edge weight to answer "what is the minimum spanning weight to connect u and v?"

items: Kruskal's MST: sort edges, DSU to detect cycles
**Min bottleneck** between two nodes = max edge weight on their MST path
Binary search on edge weight w: add all edges <= w, check if u and v are connected
Alternatively, build MST offline and use LCA/path queries

solved.title: Min Bottleneck Path (BS + DSU)
solved.statement: Given a weighted graph, for each query (u, v): find the minimum possible maximum edge weight on any path from u to v.

items: Min bottleneck path = max edge on MST path between u and v
To answer queries: sort edges, for each query binary search on edge weight, add all edges <= mid via DSU, check if u and v are connected
Better: build MST (Kruskal's), answer is max edge weight on MST path
